title: Generative artificial intelligence-supported programming education: Effects on learning performance, self-efficacy and processes
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, improves programming education outcomes and how it shapes students’ learning processes. The authors focus on four questions: whether GenAI improves programming output quality and knowledge transfer, whether it affects programming self-efficacy, how it changes students’ programming behaviours, and how different behaviour patterns under GenAI relate to academic performance. The study responds to mixed prior findings suggesting that GenAI may improve immediate task performance but may not always support deeper learning.

The intervention was a quasi-experiment in which one group of students used a ChatGPT-based platform (ChatGPT-Next-Web using GPT-3.5-turbo) for self-directed programming learning, while a control group used other Internet resources instead of GenAI. Both groups completed the same Turtle-library programming learning tasks in a standardized computer lab setting. Measures included ratings of programming products across multiple dimensions, pre/post programming self-efficacy surveys, and fine-grained behavioural trace data captured through scripts and analysed with frequency analysis, process mining, and clustering.

Participants were 55 undergraduate Physics Education students at a public university in China. All had prior foundational Python experience but were new to the Python Turtle library. The experimental activity itself lasted 120 minutes, followed by a 40-minute post-test task completed without external resources. The study took place in university computer labs with uniform hardware, and the authors also provided the experimental group with a GenAI user guide to support interaction with the tool.

The main conclusions are that GenAI support improved short-term programming performance and increased self-efficacy, especially in self-regulation and complex programming tasks, but did not improve longer-term knowledge transfer when students later had to work without external resources. Behavioural analyses showed that GenAI-supported learners relied more on information retrieval and copying, whereas control students engaged more in independent coding and code revision. Within the GenAI group, higher-performing students used the tool more critically and interactively, showing greater epistemic agency, while lower-performing students were more likely to copy outputs directly. The authors argue that GenAI can be beneficial for programming education, but only when instructional design discourages over-reliance and supports active cognitive engagement.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model used to generate natural-language responses and code-related assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in the experimental group used a simplified ChatGPT-Next-Web platform running GPT-3.5-turbo as the sole external support for self-directed Python Turtle programming learning, asking questions and receiving feedback/help during a 120-minute learning phase.

findings.finding_summary: In the practice phase, the ChatGPT-supported experimental group outperformed the control group on overall programming product quality. Median exercise-program scores were 22.30 for the experimental group versus 18.75 for the control group, with a significant Mann-Whitney difference (Z = -5.129, p = 0.000).
findings.measure: Exercise programme overall score based on six-dimension programming evaluation framework

findings.finding_summary: On the post-test programming tasks completed without external resources, there was no significant overall score difference between groups despite a slightly higher experimental-group mean. The Mann-Whitney test for test-program scores was non-significant (Z = -0.615, p = 0.538).
findings.measure: Test programme overall score completed without external resources

findings.finding_summary: For exercise-program dimensions, the ChatGPT group scored significantly higher on algorithm design (Z = -3.757, p = 0.000), code structure (Z = -3.975, p = 0.000), and code style (Z = -5.439, p = 0.000), with no significant differences on correct syntax, logical correctness, or functionality completeness. For test-program dimensions, the ChatGPT group retained an advantage only in code style (Z = -3.899, p = 0.000) but performed significantly worse on logical correctness (Z = -2.245, p = 0.025) and functionality completeness (Z = -2.319, p = 0.020).
findings.measure: Programming product subdimension scores: correct syntax, logical correctness, functionality completeness, algorithm design, code structure, code style

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT support significantly improved programming self-efficacy in two post-test dimensions. Compared with the control group, the experimental group scored higher on self-regulation (t = 2.778, df = 52, p = 0.008) and complex programming tasks (t = 2.550, df = 52, p = 0.014), while no significant difference was found for independence and persistence (t = 1.125, df = 52, p = 0.266).
findings.measure: Programming self-efficacy scale post-test dimensions: self-regulation, complex programming tasks, independence and persistence

findings.finding_summary: Within the ChatGPT group, clustered behavior patterns were associated with different post-test outcomes. Type 2 learners had significantly higher post-test scores than Type 1 learners (Mean = 19.34 vs 16.13; Mann-Whitney U = 48.50, Z = -2.065, p = 0.039), while learning gain differences were not significant; higher-performing learners more often questioned, evaluated, and selectively applied AI output, whereas lower-performing learners more often copied generated code directly.
findings.measure: Post-test score and learning gain by clustered learning-behavior pattern within experimental group

quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental study with pretest/posttest group comparison and detailed behavioral/process data, but it is not a randomized trial and uses a relatively small sample from one university context.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear positive short-term effects on practice performance and self-efficacy, but no overall post-test advantage and some negative transfer effects on logical correctness and functionality without AI support. Because effect sizes are not reported and impacts are mixed across outcomes, overall impact is best classified as unclear/modest.
